analysis.one_liner: Restricts how employers can surveil, collect, and sell data on their workers.
analysis.headline: Introduced in the Senate on June 18, 2026 with 8 Democratic and independent sponsors, then referred to the Senate labor committee, where no further action has been taken.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would sharply limit what employers can do with workplace surveillance. It would ban monitoring aimed at identifying union activity, political or religious views, health conditions, or whistleblowers; bar collecting data while workers are off duty or in sensitive areas like restrooms and break rooms; and prohibit selling worker data to third parties. It would also require employers to disclose what data they collect and how it affects decisions about hiring, firing, and pay, let workers see and correct their own data, create a new Worker Protection and Technology Division at the Labor Department to enforce the rules, and give workers and unions the right to sue violators with statutory damages.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers at employers with 11 or more employees, including applicants and remote workers, and the unions that represent them. They would gain limits on keystroke, biometric, location, and off-duty monitoring, the right to know what data their boss collects and correct errors in it, and the right to sue without being forced into arbitration.

how_it_helps.text: Bans using employee data to identify or monitor workers' union activity, political or religious views, health status, immigration status, or plans to report the employer for breaking the law [S2]
Prohibits collecting data on off-duty workers, including in restrooms, locker rooms, lactation rooms, and workers' homes, and prohibits selling or licensing worker data to any third party [S2]

Requires employers to disclose in plain language what worker data they collect, how, how often, who has access, and how it feeds work-related decisions; workers can obtain their data within 30 days and have errors corrected, and can demand reconsideration of a work decision based on wrong data [S2]

Creates a Worker Protection and Technology Division within the Labor Department with an Administrator, technologist staff, and advisory boards including labor representatives, to investigate complaints and issue orders [S2]

Gives workers and unions a private right to sue for violations with statutory damages (up to $40,000 for repeated data-minimization violations and up to $100,000 for willful retaliation), attorney's fees, and protection from retaliation for exercising these rights; predispute arbitration and class-action waivers would be unenforceable for these claims, and state attorneys general and privacy regulators could also sue [S2]

analysis.who_pays: Employers with 11 or more employees, who face compliance, disclosure, and data-deletion duties and new litigation exposure, and the worker-surveillance technology industry, whose products would be restricted or banned.

drawbacks.text: The threshold applies to employers with just 11 workers, so small businesses would bear disclosure, recordkeeping, and data-deletion costs for ordinary human-resources information along with large corporations [S2]

The definition of employee data is extremely broad, covering everything from productivity metrics to IP addresses, and the private right of action carries statutory damages of $5,000 to $40,000 per violation, which could produce lawsuits over routine recordkeeping and administrative slips rather than serious surveillance [S2]

Restrictions on collecting data 'related to' union or protected activity, and bans on off-duty monitoring including at home, could be difficult to apply where remote work blends personal and work devices and where employers must lawfully respond to workplace disputes [S2]
The 'least invasive means' and 'strictly necessary' standards for permissible data collection are subjective and would require case-by-case interpretation by a newly created regulator [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core protections target documented practices — productivity scoring, biometric tracking, off-duty social-media monitoring, algorithmic firing — that workers currently have little power to see or contest, so the benefits are real. But the bill is drafted very broadly: an 11-employee threshold, an all-encompassing data definition, and high statutory damages would impose significant compliance and litigation costs on employers of every size, and some of that cost would fall on small businesses handling ordinary HR files. A narrower version targeting the worst surveillance practices would preserve most of the benefit at a fraction of the cost.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee; no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled, and the Congress runs through January 3, 2027.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Markey introduced the bill on June 18, 2026, joined by seven Democratic and independent colleagues: Schatz, Sanders, Baldwin, Warren, Blumenthal, Fetterman, and Booker [S1][S4]
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day of introduction; the action history shows no further steps [S4]
No Republican senator has cosponsored the bill, and the committee it sits in is chaired by the opposing party [S3]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has moved: the practices the bill would restrict — including selling worker data and monitoring union activity — remain legal at the federal level, and the employers and vendors that rely on them face no new obligations.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and surveillance vendors, so far

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and shepherded it to introduction with seven colleagues

for.name: Sens. Schatz, Sanders, Baldwin, Warren, Blumenthal, Fetterman, and Booker
for.what_they_did: Joined as original cosponsors at introduction, giving the bill its full 8-sponsor bloc

against.name: Sen. Bill Cassidy
against.role: Chair, Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair of the committee to which the bill was referred, has taken no action to schedule a hearing or markup; the bill has sat without a calendar slot since referral

sides.party_line_note: All 8 sponsors are Democrats or an independent who caucuses with Democrats; no Republican has cosponsored, and the bill was referred to a committee chaired by a Republican.

industries.note: The bill bans or tightly restricts their core products: productivity and behavior scoring, biometric tracking, off-duty monitoring, and sale of worker data. Their revenue currently comes from charging employers to watch workers, so their interest runs against the workers being watched [S2]

Companies that rate, rank, and deactivate workers by automated systems would have to disclose the data behind those decisions and let workers correct it and demand reconsideration, and could no longer enforce arbitration clauses for these claims [S2]

industries.industry: HR data brokers and employee-data resellers
industries.note: The bill prohibits selling or licensing employee data to third parties and requires opt-in consent for transfers even to service providers, cutting off a market in worker information [S2]
Unions gain a private right to sue over surveillance aimed at organizing activity and would hold seats on the new Labor Advisory Board at the Labor Department [S2]

analysis.trajectory: With only Democratic sponsorship, a Republican-controlled Senate, and no hearing scheduled after referral, the bill's realistic path is to sit in committee for the rest of the Congress. Its best chance would be having provisions attached to a larger, must-pass package, which is uncommon for a bill at this stage.
